summary: Space Cadet Mission is a cooperative game built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 Space Mission Design Game challenge. Up to four players share one room and one spacecraft. The commander picks a real launch site and destination, with facts drawn from NASA and partner missions such as Apollo, Artemis, Landsat, the ISS, Gateway, and Webb. The scientist reviews power, batteries, and instruments for that route and reads the past week of solar activity from NASA’s DONKI catalog. Communications holds the trajectory and matches the radio wave. The engineer builds the rocket on a 15 by 15 grid, balancing mass, fuel, power, crew, cost, and heat shielding. Those decisions then fly together: fuel, shielding, and solar storms decide whether the ship makes it. Players stay in sync over MQTT, and each role only controls its own station. The project matters because students rarely get to run a mission from concept to flight. Here every trade-off has a consequence, and every course is tied to a real launch.
details:
What it does and how it works

Space Cadet Mission is a cooperative game in which up to four players design and fly one spacecraft together. They join a shared room with a code. Each person takes one station, and the mission only advances when that station finishes its job.

The commander chooses a real launch site and a destination. Sites include Kennedy, Vandenberg, Wallops, Poker Flat, Baikonur, Kourou, Tanegashima, and Sriharikota. Each card explains what actually flies from that pad, with links to NASA and partner sources: Apollo and Artemis landings, Landsat, Cygnus cargo to the ISS, Gateway’s near-rectilinear halo orbit, and James Webb.

The scientist reviews the route. Power, batteries, instruments, and stores change with the destination. A sunlit mare can fly on panels and one battery. Shackleton needs a wing and a generator because the crater stays dark. A far-side landing needs a dish because Earth never rises. The scientist also reads the last seven days of solar activity from NASA’s DONKI catalog: flares, coronal mass ejections, and geomagnetic storms.

Communications then holds the trajectory, confirms a Morse message, and aligns the radio wave by matching height, speed, and phase to a guide signal.

The engineer builds the rocket on a 15×15 grid. Parts have mass, cost, fuel, power, crew seats, stores, and drag. The allowed kit is different for every course, so a polar Earth satellite and a four-person Gateway flight cannot be built the same way. A blueprint clears only when it meets that course.

The crew then flies the ship together. Fuel, shielding, and solar storms decide whether it arrives. Rooms stay in sync over MQTT, so each phone or computer is only its own station.

Benefits

Players practice the real limits of a mission: objective, launch site, mass, power, communications, and operations. A heavier kit, a missing antenna, or a weak power system is not a lecture. It blocks the blueprint or fails the flight. Live DONKI data ties the game to space weather that is happening now, and every destination points back to a published mission.

Intended impact

The game is for students and first-time players who rarely get to run a mission from concept to flight. The aim is to make engineering trade-offs tangible and to show that launch site, spacecraft design, and the Sun all change the outcome. A classroom or a friend group can share one room, each person owning a different job the way a real crew does.

Tools and software

The app is written in TypeScript with React Native and Expo SDK 58, using Expo Router, and it runs in the browser on phones and computers. No custom hardware is required. Multiplayer uses MQTT through a public HiveMQ broker. Solar activity comes from the NASA CCMC DONKI API. The interface uses React Native SVG. Audio uses expo-audio. The interface is available in English, Russian, and Kazakh.

Creativity

Mission control is staged as a desktop the crew shares, with each job in its own window. The four stations unlock in order, so design, science, communications, and flight stay separate. Engineering budgets are written per destination instead of one generic rocket. Communications is played as Morse and as a wave the player has to lay on top of a guide. Space weather is read from the current DONKI week, not from a fixed script.

What the team considered

The team treated the challenge limits as the rules of the game: mission objective, spacecraft parts, instruments, launch vehicle, power, mass, communications, and where the ship is going. Crewed lunar flights, polar Earth satellites, cargo runs to the station, and far-side landings each demand a different kit. Facts stay attached to real NASA and partner pages, including cases where a pad and a destination do not match how that agency actually flies. Language support covers the team’s players. Cooperation matters because no single station can both choose the course and build the ship.
